stem: Which statement summarises the Prometheus alerting guidance?

options.text: Keep alerting simple, alert on symptoms, have good dashboards for causes, and avoid pages with nothing to do
options.note: Right. That's the guide's own summary.

options.text: Alert on every possible cause so nothing is missed
options.note: That leads to alert fatigue. Aim for as few alerts as possible.

options.text: Page on every metric that crosses a static threshold
options.note: Thresholds on causes create noise. Page on user-facing symptoms.

options.text: Avoid alerting and rely on dashboards
options.note: Alerts are essential. They just need to be the right ones.

explanation: To summarise: keep alerting simple, alert on symptoms, have good consoles to pinpoint causes, and avoid having pages where there is nothing to do.
hint: The guide condenses it into one sentence.

stem: Which of these should page an on-call engineer?

options.text: 5% of checkout requests are failing for users
options.note: Right. A user-visible symptom that needs action.

options.text: A database server's CPU is at 90% but latency is normal
options.note: That's a cause with no user impact. Put it on a dashboard or in a ticket queue.

options.text: Disk usage on one node rose by 2% today
options.note: Not urgent. At most a capacity ticket.

options.text: A lower-level service is a bit slow, but user latency is fine
options.note: The docs say no need to page if overall user latency is fine.

explanation: Alert on symptoms associated with end-user pain, not every possible cause. Cause-based alerts are for troubleshooting and shouldn't wake anyone.

stem: According to the Zen of Prometheus, alerts should be… (select all that apply)

options.text: Urgent
options.note: Right. One of the four qualities.

options.text: Actionable
options.note: Right. Someone must be able to do something.

options.text: Real
options.note: Right. Not false positives.

options.text: As numerous as possible for full coverage
options.note: The opposite. Don't over-alert, because alert fatigue is real.

explanation: Alerts should be urgent, important, actionable and real. Don't over-alert: alert fatigue is real.
hint: Four adjectives are listed. One option contradicts them.

sources.title: Zen › Alerts should be urgent, important, actionable, and real

stem: For an online serving system, where does the guide recommend alerting on latency and errors?

options.text: As high up in the stack as possible, paging on latency at only one point
options.note: Right. Lower layers being slow doesn't matter if users are fine.

options.text: On every microservice separately
options.note: That multiplies pages for the same user problem.

options.text: Only at the database layer
options.note: The guidance is as high up the stack, close to users, as possible.

options.text: Only on CPU usage
options.note: CPU is a cause, not a symptom.

explanation: Typically alert on high latency and error rates as high up in the stack as possible. Only page on latency at one point in a stack.

stem: A batch job runs every 4 hours and takes about 1 hour. Roughly what "no success since" threshold does the guide suggest for paging?

options.text: About 10 hours, allowing for 2 full runs
options.note: Right. That's the docs' exact example.

options.text: 4 hours, one run period
options.note: A single failed run shouldn't need a human. Allow at least two runs.

options.text: 1 hour, the job's runtime
options.note: Far too sensitive.

options.text: A week
options.note: Too slow to catch real problems.

explanation: Page if the batch job hasn't succeeded recently enough to cause user-visible problems, generally at least enough time for 2 full runs. For a job every 4 hours taking an hour, 10 hours would be reasonable.
hint: Two full runs plus the runtime.

stem: What is the key thing to alert on for offline processing systems?

options.text: How long data takes to get through the system
options.note: Right. Page when the delay gets high enough to affect users.

options.text: The number of requests in progress
options.note: That's more of an online-serving metric, and it isn't the key alert.

options.text: Whether the process restarted
options.note: Restarts alone aren't user impact.

options.text: CPU usage of each stage
options.note: That's a cause signal.

explanation: For offline processing systems, the key metric is how long data takes to get through the system, so page if that gets high enough to cause user impact.
hint: No one waits for a response, but data freshness matters.

stem: Why should alerting rules usually have a for duration, such as 5 minutes?

options.text: So brief blips, like one failed scrape, don't fire an alert
options.note: Right. The Zen's rule of thumb is at least 5 minutes.

options.text: To delay notifications until business hours
options.note: for is about how long the condition holds, not time of day.

options.text: Because rules are only evaluated every 5 minutes
options.note: Evaluation follows evaluation_interval. for is separate.

options.text: To make alerts resolve faster
options.note: for delays firing. It doesn't speed up resolving.

explanation: Without a for duration, a single failed scrape could cause an alert to fire. You need tolerance. As a rule of thumb, use at least 5 minutes.

options.text: Monitoring that your monitoring stack (Prometheus, Alertmanager, Pushgateway…) is working
options.note: Right. Ideally with an end-to-end check.

options.text: Monitoring the metadata labels of series
options.note: It's about the health of the monitoring system itself.

options.text: Monitoring other companies' services
options.note: Not what the term means.

options.text: Aggregating metrics from several Prometheus servers
options.note: That's federation or long-term storage.

explanation: Have alerts to ensure that Prometheus servers, Alertmanagers, Pushgateways and other monitoring infrastructure are available and working correctly.

stem: Which metamonitoring approach does the guide prefer?

options.text: A blackbox test that an alert travels from Pushgateway to Prometheus to Alertmanager to email
options.note: Right. One end-to-end symptom check beats many component alerts.

options.text: A separate alert on every monitoring component's CPU
options.note: Those are causes. The guide prefers end-to-end symptoms.

options.text: No alerts, since monitoring rarely fails
options.note: You need confidence that monitoring works.

options.text: Asking users to report outages
options.note: That's the opposite of monitoring.

explanation: Prefer symptoms: a blackbox test that alerts get from Pushgateway to Prometheus to Alertmanager to email is better than individual alerts on each component.
hint: Same symptom-first idea, applied to the monitoring itself.

stem: What is the minimum the Zen of Prometheus says you should alert on for anything you run?

options.text: Presence and health of your targets, using the up metric
options.note: Right. Prometheus generates up for every target.

options.text: Every log line containing ERROR
options.note: That would be noisy, and it isn't the stated minimum.

options.text: Memory usage above 50%
options.note: That's an arbitrary cause threshold.

options.text: Nothing until users complain
options.note: The Zen says if you run it, put an alert on it.

explanation: Always have an alert, at least, on the presence and health of your targets. Prometheus generates the up metric automatically for each target. Use it.
hint: Which metric does every scrape create?

sources.title: Zen › If you run it, then you should put an alert on it

stem: What naming convention has the community settled on for alert names?

options.text: CamelCase, such as InstanceDown
options.note: Right. No strict rule, but CamelCase is the convention.

options.text: snake_case with a _total suffix
options.note: That's for counter metrics, not alert names.

options.text: ALL_CAPS
options.note: Not the convention.

options.text: level:metric:operations
options.note: That's the recording rule naming convention.

explanation: There are no strict restrictions on alert names, but the community has rallied around CamelCase.
hint: Think of a well-known example alert.
